node_sequence.text: Has the person attempted a medically serious act of self-harm? (Check for signs of poisoning/intoxication, bleeding from self-inflicted wound, loss of consciousness, or extreme lethargy)

Is there an imminent risk of self-harm/suicide? (Current thoughts/plan of self-harm/suicide, or history of thoughts/plan in the past month or act in the past year in a person who is now extremely agitated, violent, distressed or lacks communication)
Is there a history of thoughts or plan of self-harm in the past month or act of self-harm in the past year?
Does the person have concurrent MNS conditions? (Depression, Disorders due to substance use, Child & adolescent mental and behavioral disorders, Psychoses, Epilepsy)
Does the person have chronic pain?

Does the person have emotional symptoms severe enough to warrant clinical management? (Difficulty carrying out usual activities, repeated self-medication for emotional distress, unexplained physical symptoms, marked distress or repeated help-seeking)
Go to Other Significant Mental Health Complaints module.
Is there a physical cause that fully explains the presenting symptoms?
Is this depression or another MNS condition discussed in another module of this guide?
Is the person seeking help to relieve symptoms or having considerable difficulty with daily functioning because of their symptoms?
Other Significant Mental Health Complaints are likely.
Is there imminent risk of suicide?
Has the person been exposed to extreme stressors? (e.g., physical or sexual violence, major accidents, bereavement or other major losses)

Apply Protocol 1: Do not prescribe anti-anxiety or antidepressant medicines unless advised by a specialist. Reduce stress, teach relaxation techniques, and strengthen social supports (ECP). Acknowledge symptoms but avoid unnecessary investigations; explain that no serious disease has been identified. Encourage return to daily activities. Follow-up: Ask the person to return in 2-4 weeks if symptoms do not improve or worsen. If improving, continue treatment plan. If not improving or if insisting on further investigations, review Protocol 1 and consider consulting a specialist.

cases.user_story:
Shamsun Nahar, a 34-year-old tailoring supervisor from Sonadanga, Khulna, comes to the upazila health complex after three weeks of sudden chest tightness, trembling, “air hunger,” and stomach fluttering whenever she thinks about delayed garment orders and rising household expenses. She has visited two pharmacies and a local doctor already; antacids, vitamins, and repeated blood pressure checks have not reassured her for long. Her pulse, blood pressure, glucose, hemoglobin, thyroid screening, and ECG are normal, and she has no fever, weight loss, injury, or medical illness that explains the episodes.

She is embarrassed that the symptoms have begun interfering with her work: she has missed two shifts, avoids supervising the cutting room when it feels crowded, and asks her younger sister to accompany her on rickshaw rides because she fears another spell. She still enjoys evening tea with her children and watching dramas with her mother-in-law, eats normally, and says she wants to “get steady again,” not disappear from life. She denies feeling persistently hopeless or depressed, has no hallucinations, unusual beliefs, seizures, alcohol or drug use, or history of mental health treatment. She is 34, not an adolescent, and her family describes her as communicative, calm, and cooperative, though visibly worried.

When asked privately, Shamsun clearly says she has never swallowed poison, cut herself, tried hanging, or harmed herself in any way; there are no wounds, intoxication, lethargy, or loss of consciousness. She denies any current wish to die, any plan to hurt herself, and any suicidal thoughts in the past month or self-harm in the past year. She has ordinary financial stress but no recent bereavement, assault, major accident, displacement, or other extreme traumatic event. She also denies chronic pain, saying her body aches only briefly after long sewing shifts and resolves with rest. Her main request is help controlling the frightening physical sensations and worry so she can return to work and manage her household normally.
